source.title: Synthetic Persona Pretraining: Alignment from Token Zero

page_placements.theme: Pretraining and midtraining history affect later safety

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a full LessWrong post, including appendices and comments. It notes that a later paper has been released, but that does not make the supplied post incomplete.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports its own results for a new pretraining-time alignment intervention and evaluates the resulting models on adversarial safety benchmarks. This extends the shallow-alignment and bypass discussion to a new intervention and training stage; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or token-position measurements.
record.gate_note: The post cites prior findings about benign fine-tuning, refusal directions, and alignment depth, but these are background claims, not results of this study. Its own safety evaluation includes adversarial methods such as GCG/DSN suffixes and PEZ, but the prose reports mostly aggregate benchmark results rather than attack-specific outcomes. It does not test compliant prefills or decoding changes. Persona-binding citation rates and general-capability scores are not harmful-request compliance measures.
record.test_reason: The post uses shallow post-training alignment (citing Qi et al. 2023/2025) as motivation for a pretraining intervention (SPP). Its own results compare SPP models with data-matched baselines on a five-benchmark jailbreak ASR aggregate, plus abliteration and persona-binding probes. That is the study's own method compared with others, not a test of any version. Suffix attacks (GCG, DSN within JBB; PEZ) sit inside the aggregate, but only figure-only per-benchmark results exist. The attacks are cached transfers from vicuna-13b (JBB) or PEZ runs on 1.7B from-scratch models, so whether they defeat refusal cannot be read. No harmful or benign fine-tuning, prefilling, per-token KL or position-wise analysis is run. The authors say benign fine-tuning robustness was not evaluated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that SPP models are consistently safer than data-matched baselines, especially on worst-case (max) ASR, and that token-zero injection beats midtraining. They add that values transfer to held-out charter articles (persona binding), and that this binding is brittle to template mismatch. Filtering alone does not help. Abliteration most easily removes SPP's safety, suggesting a well-defined linear direction. Results are preliminary at 1.7B parameters and 100B tokens.
record.recipe_differences: The referenced studies concern post-training fine-tuning and response-token depth. This post instead adds synthetic reflections to pretraining documents, comparing token-zero pretraining with midtraining and several post-training/template setups.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety gains depended on whether the post-training assistant token matched the pretraining token. Reflection placement, reflection point of view, and whether context loss was included also affected ASR in the study's ablations. Evaluations used zero temperature.

fits_no_version.finding: Appending first-person moral reflections to 10% of pretraining documents lowered mean jailbreak ASR to 1.7%, reported as 63% below a data-matched 1.7B baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining-time value annotation reduces jailbreak susceptibility of small post-trained models relative to data-matched baselines.

fits_no_version.finding: SPP's safety benefit vanished (+8% ASR) when the post-training assistant token differed from the pretraining one.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining-installed safety transfers only when the post-training template matches the pretraining assistant token.

fits_no_version.finding: Projecting out the refusal direction raised ASR most for the SPP model on JBB direct and PAP prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining-installed safety can concentrate in a single removable activation direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Toxicity-filtered pretraining was the same or slightly less safe than unfiltered pretraining.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Filtering toxic pretraining data does not by itself improve jailbreak robustness.

record.peer_reviewed: LessWrong post; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The authors characterize the results as preliminary and limited to 1.7B parameters and 100B tokens. They state that benign fine-tuning robustness was not evaluated. Some reported confidence intervals overlap, and the supplied prose does not give exact values for many plotted results. Several percentage reductions are inconsistent within the post. The five-benchmark aggregate does not identify the outcome for individual suffix attacks.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows were added for every benchmark or SPP design ablation: the supplied text describes their plots and some qualitative comparisons but does not provide attack-specific numerical results in prose, and those ablations do not test a listed claim version. Persona-binding citation rates and general-capability results were left out because they are not harmful-request compliance or bypass measures.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning is performed; the post only cites prior results.
Benign fine-tuning is explicitly not evaluated (Limitations).
No per-token KL or response-position analysis. 'Token Zero' refers to the pretraining start, not response positions.
No prefilling or decoding attacks. Suffix attacks are only folded into an aggregate; per-benchmark results are figure-only.
No weight or rank localization. Abliteration concerns an activation direction.
Shallowness is not attributed to data or objective by any experiment.
SPP is not evaluated for safety depth across response tokens, nor under fine-tuning attacks.

missing.what: Per-benchmark ASR, including JBB's GCG and DSN suffix methods and PEZ suffix attacks, for each model. Needed to see whether suffix attacks defeat refusal in these models.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong work-in-progress post; a later full paper exists (arXiv 2608.13482). The shallow-alignment claim is premise and motivation, not tested. Relative-reduction figures are internally inconsistent (60/62/71% and 63/64%). A commenter notes PAP baseline ASR is 0%, the evals are saturated, and the token-zero vs midtraining and filtered vs baseline differences are not significant; the authors concede some confidence intervals overlap.

versions.untested_parts: The post cites prior harmful fine-tuning results but does not fine-tune its models on harmful examples to measure harmful-request compliance.
The post explicitly says it has not evaluated benign fine-tuning attacks or continued fine-tuning.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis is reported. ‘Token Zero’ refers to when pretraining reflections are introduced, not response-token positions.

The study evaluates aggregate ASR on a suite that includes suffix-based attacks, but does not report the suffix-specific rates in prose. It does not test compliant-token prefilling or decoding changes.
The abliteration experiment removes a refusal direction in activation space; it does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety.
The post argues for pretraining-time alignment and tests SPP, but does not test whether data or a training objective causes safety to be shallow in response-token positions.
SPP and midtraining are compared as alignment interventions, but the study does not train or measure safety distributed beyond the first response tokens, nor test whether such deepening holds up.

relation.reason: Shallow post-training alignment is an explicit premise motivating the pretraining intervention; the reported comparisons do not independently test the listed claim versions.

tranche.reason: The post motivates SPP using prior shallow-alignment findings and reports its own intervention's performance. It does not measure response-token safety depth, safety localization in weights or ranks, or fine-tuning erosion.

source_check.notes: The rows correctly preserve inconsistent reductions: PB-SFT 63%/64%; aligned mixSFT 62%/60%/71%. Template-mismatch loss of benefit was demonstrated with mixSFT; robustness to continued or benign fine-tuning was explicitly untested.
